Essential Evidence Map

Phage receptor / host-range analysis — Pseudomonas phage therapy (iGEM)

Published

July 5, 2026

NoteWhat this document is

A standalone walkthrough of the key files behind our phage–host analysis: what each is, what it shows, and how they chain together. Figures and table snippets are embedded and numbered. Source files: code/output/0703_phage_host_matrix/.

1 What we are doing

We are a phage-therapy project working with several sequenced Pseudomonas isolates (9-6-2, 9-2-1, 10-10-2, 8-5-2, 8-10-2). The goal is to determine which surface receptor our phages target on these bacteria. Our own lytic phages are isolated (plaques) but not yet sequenced, so we cannot read their receptor-binding proteins (RBPs) directly.

We therefore bridge indirectly:

  1. Catalogue each isolate’s surface receptors (Section 2.1).
  2. Ask which known Pseudomonas phages (from the PharBP database) infect strains that share those receptors (Section 2.2, Section 2.3) — a clue for which phages / RBP classes could target our isolates.
  3. Attempt structural folding (RBP × receptor) to sharpen the clue (Section 3) — which proved non-informative and is reported as a controlled negative result (Section 3.3).

2 Part A — Our receptors and who shares them

The primary, clue-level evidence. Does not depend on the folding step in Part B.

2.1 Our receptor catalogue

receptor_by_strain.tsv organizes all isolates’ receptors into 144 unique receptor groups, marking overlap across isolates. Groups present in all 5 isolates (core) = 43; groups present only in 8-10-2 = 46 — a candidate driver of a difference in host range (Table 1).

2.2 The PharBP host list

pharbp_pseudomonas_hosts.tsv: from 6,376 Pseudomonas host entries on PharBP there are 43 unique genomes (54 named strains; the rest are unspecified “Pseudomonas” and unusable). P. putida KT2440 stands out — many phages (Table 2).

2.3 Our receptors × PharBP strains

receptor_host_presence.tsv combines Table 1 and Table 2: how our receptors are present across the 54 PharBP strains (# host strains matching at ≥90 / ≥70 / ≥50 % identity, best host, etc.). This is the key intermediate for indirectly predicting the RBP range for our isolates (Table 3).

TipPart A takeaway

We now know the list of our receptors that appear in PharBP, and the hosts that share the same receptors — the clue-level readout our PI accepted.

2.4 The RBP-side view

The same information from the RBP angle (Figure 2): reference strains from PharBP (left) and the exact RBPs that bind a given strain (right).

3 Part B — The folding attempt and why it is a negative result

Because both candidate lists were large, we condensed them: for RBPs we kept a representative of each highly-similar cluster (>90 %); for receptors we kept only plausible phage targets (removed efflux pumps etc.).

3.1 Condensed candidate lists

condensed_rbps.tsv → 114 RBPs; condensed_receptors.tsv → 63 receptors (Table 4, Table 5).

3.2 The simulation

binding_matrix.csv holds all 7,182 pairs predicted by ESMFold (6,358 folded OK + 824 skipped for length). iptm = interaction/binding score; ptm = folding quality; status = skipped-or-not (Table 6). Large biases follow.

3.3 Control test for ESMFold

The matrix gave suspiciously flat scores (everything near 0.13) and the top “hits” tracked protein size, not any specific pairing. A screen is only meaningful if it can separate a real binder from a non-binder, so we tested the method against pairs with known answers.

Hypothesis.

  • H1 (method works): documented binders should score above their scrambled/mismatched controls and above the screen background.
  • H0 (null): the score reflects generic foldability/size, so real ≈ scrambled ≈ background.

The three positive controls — experimentally documented pairs, prioritizing solved co-structures (ground truth) plus one in our own organism; sequences from UniProt/NCBI (Table 7).

For each positive we also folded a length-matched scrambled receptor (same residues, shuffled — removes the size confound) and a mismatched receptor, through the identical pipeline (Figure 5, Table 8).

ImportantConclusion — H0 supported, H1 rejected

Known binders did not separate from controls (the gold-standard pb5 × FhuA differs from its own scrambled receptor by 0.001). Whole-complex pTM collapses on scrambling but the interface ipTM does not move → the score is not reading a real interface. The folding screen is not informative for RBP–receptor binding, and we do not use it as evidence. Our receptor-repertoire overlap (Part A) remains the primary, clue-level readout and does not depend on this step.
